body:
Why reliable data matters

Disaster decisions are often made under time pressure. Yet an apparently precise map, photograph or automated assessment can still contain errors. Data quality therefore matters as much as the speed at which information is collected.

For example, a detailed map prepared before a major flood may not show a road that has become submerged. An old photograph shared during an emergency may create a false impression of current conditions. Information must be judged in relation to its source, time, accuracy and purpose.

Important dimensions of data quality

  • Accuracy: Whether the observation correctly describes the condition or location.
  • Timeliness: Whether the information is recent enough for the decision.
  • Completeness: Whether important people, places or observations are missing.
  • Consistency: Whether information from different sources can be compared without contradictions caused by definitions or formats.
  • Traceability: Whether users can identify the source, date and method by which information was obtained.

A map can be geographically accurate but unsuitable for an urgent decision because it is outdated. Similarly, a large number of reports does not necessarily mean that the reports are representative or reliable.

Verification and misinformation

Digital platforms can spread useful information rapidly. They can also spread rumours, altered images and unverified claims. Authorities should separate reported conditions from verified conditions and clearly mark uncertainty when information is incomplete.

Cross-checking satellite imagery, local reports and information from responsible departments can improve confidence. However, different sources may observe the same event at different times, so an apparent disagreement does not always mean that one source is false.

Privacy and protection of personal information

Disaster applications may collect names, contact details, precise locations, photographs or information about people needing assistance. Such information can be important for helping affected residents, but unnecessary disclosure can expose people to additional harm.

Responsible data handling follows several basic principles:

  • Purpose limitation: Collect information for a clear and legitimate disaster management purpose.
  • Data minimisation: Collect only the personal information reasonably needed for that purpose.
  • Restricted access: Allow access according to legitimate responsibilities rather than making sensitive details publicly available.
  • Security: Protect records against unauthorised access, alteration and disclosure.
  • Retention control: Avoid keeping identifiable personal information longer than justified by the purpose and applicable requirements.

For instance, a public map may need to show the number of people requiring assistance in an area without displaying every person's name or precise home address.

Bias and unequal access

Digital exclusion occurs when people cannot benefit equally from digital systems because of limited connectivity, inaccessible interfaces, language barriers, disability, low digital literacy or lack of devices.

AI-based assessments can also become biased when training data do not adequately represent certain locations, buildings or communities. A model that performs well in cities may need additional validation before being used in rural or remote environments.

Authorities should therefore combine digital tools with local knowledge and accessible communication. Important warnings may require multiple languages, suitable accessible formats and non-digital channels.

Accountability and human judgement

For decisions affecting human safety, it should be clear which institution is responsible, what evidence supports the decision and how errors can be corrected. Automated systems may support analysis but should not obscure the role of accountable officials.

Information systems should also be prepared for power cuts, network failures and cybersecurity incidents. Secure backups, alternative communication methods and tested procedures help maintain continuity when digital infrastructure is disrupted.

Prelims focus

  • Data quality includes accuracy, timeliness, completeness, consistency and traceability.
  • Geotagged information may still have an incorrect location or timestamp.
  • Data minimisation limits collection of unnecessary personal information.
  • Digital exclusion can prevent vulnerable communities from receiving warnings.
  • Human oversight and accountability are important in AI-supported decisions.
  • Trap: More data or a more detailed map does not necessarily mean more reliable information.

[Sources: UNDRR and partner organisations, Leveraging AI to Enhance Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems, 2026, recommendations on human oversight, equity and governance; UNDRR, Inclusive Early Warning Early Action: Checklist and Implementation Guide, 2023, overview; NRSC, Bhuvan Mobile Applications, field-data collection and authentication sections; consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Satellite observations, field reports and automated assessments pass five quality checks; uncertainty stays marked, while reviewed information supports accountable decisions.
pictures.caption: Information should pass essential quality checks before it supports important disaster decisions.

title: Data Quality, Privacy, Digital Inclusion and Ethical Use of Disaster Technology

body:
Meaning of capacity building

Capacity building in disaster management means developing and strengthening the knowledge, skills, resources, organisational arrangements and coordination needed to prevent, prepare for, respond to and recover from disasters.

Preparedness is not achieved simply by purchasing equipment or preparing a written plan. Staff and communities must know their roles, understand the relevant hazards and be able to act together.

Capacity building may involve public awareness programmes, technical training, practical demonstrations, exercises, community participation and improvement of institutions.

Distinguishing awareness, training and exercises

ActivityMain purposeExample
Awareness programmeImprove general understanding of risks and precautionsExplaining flood warnings to residents
TrainingDevelop knowledge or skills needed for an assigned roleTeaching staff how to communicate through an emergency contact system
ExercisePractise or test plans and coordination in a simulated situationConducting a school evacuation drill
EvaluationIdentify strengths, gaps and required improvementsReviewing whether everyone received instructions during the drill

These activities complement each other. Awareness helps people recognise danger; training helps them perform specific responsibilities; exercises show whether plans and trained personnel can function effectively together.

Types of disaster management exercises

Tabletop exercise

A tabletop exercise is discussion-based. Participants examine a simulated emergency and explain what their institutions would do. It is useful for understanding responsibilities, identifying coordination gaps and testing assumptions without physically deploying personnel or equipment.

Functional exercise

A functional exercise tests the operation of selected organisational functions, such as communication, decision-making and coordination at an Emergency Operations Centre. It does not necessarily involve a large field deployment.

Mock drill or field exercise

A mock drill involves practical performance of selected actions under a simulated emergency. For example, students and teachers may practise leaving a school by the designated route and assembling at a predetermined safe location.

A larger field or full-scale exercise may involve several participating agencies and more extensive simulated activities. Its scale is greater than that of a simple facility-level drill.

A tabletop exercise primarily tests decisions through discussion. A mock drill tests actions through practice. Both can identify weaknesses in a disaster management plan.

The four phases of disaster management exercises

India's National Disaster Management Authority has issued guidance on Disaster Management Exercises, often abbreviated as DMEx. The guidance describes a four-phase approach.

  1. Planning: Determine the hazard scenario, objectives, participating institutions, responsibilities and evaluation criteria.
  2. Preparation: Brief participants as appropriate, arrange communications and resources, and establish safety measures for the simulated activity.
  3. Conduct: Carry out the discussion or simulated actions while designated observers record what happens.
  4. Post-exercise follow-up: Examine observations, identify gaps, assign corrective actions and improve the relevant plans and arrangements.

What should an exercise evaluate?

The aim is not merely to complete a visible activity. An exercise should reveal whether the intended arrangements actually work. Depending on its objectives, evaluation may examine:

  • Whether participants knew their assigned responsibilities.
  • Whether messages reached the correct people promptly and accurately.
  • Whether different departments shared consistent information.
  • Whether designated safe routes and assembly locations were suitable.
  • Whether arrangements considered children, persons with disabilities and others needing assistance.
  • Whether problems were documented and assigned for correction.

An exercise should be conducted safely and should not create avoidable danger for participants or bystanders. Simulated emergencies are opportunities for learning, not occasions to expose people to actual hazardous conditions.

Gujarat's capacity-building institution

The Gujarat Institute of Disaster Management (GIDM), located in Gandhinagar, is an institution dedicated to training, research and capacity building in disaster risk management.

Its training approaches include residential programmes, online learning, virtual classrooms and satellite-supported communication methods. These help reach government personnel, local institutions and other stakeholders.

Prelims focus

  • Capacity building develops knowledge, skills, organisational arrangements and resources.
  • Tabletop exercises are discussion-based.
  • Mock drills involve practical simulated actions.
  • NDMA's DMEx approach has 4 phases: planning, preparation, conduct and post-exercise follow-up.
  • GIDM is Gujarat's institution for disaster management training and capacity building.
  • Trap: Conducting a drill is not the same as completing its evaluation and corrective follow-up.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Guidelines on Disaster Management Exercises by NDMA, 10 August 2025, sections on exercise types and four-phase methodology; National Disaster Response Force, School Safety and Mock Exercise, exercise-planning and tabletop-exercise topics; GIDM, Training and Capacity Building section; consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Four phases run from planning to preparation, conduct and follow-up, with improved plans and arrangements feeding into the next exercise.
pictures.caption: A useful exercise ends with improvements that can be tested during a later exercise.

title: Capacity Building, Training and Disaster Management Exercises

body:
Why institutions need different disaster plans

A disaster can affect a school, hospital and industrial facility in different ways. Each institution needs a plan based on its hazards, the people present, the services it provides and the assistance it may require.

A disaster management plan identifies relevant risks, assigns responsibilities and describes the arrangements for preparedness, communication, protective action and recovery. The plan must be understandable to its users and reviewed when circumstances change.

School disaster management plans

Schools have a special responsibility to protect children, who may not be able to recognise hazards or make safe decisions independently. School preparedness therefore depends on teachers, school management, students and coordination with local authorities.

A school disaster management plan should address the hazards relevant to the school and commonly includes:

  • Identification of possible hazards and unsafe locations.
  • Assigned responsibilities for teachers and other staff.
  • Safe evacuation arrangements and suitable assembly locations.
  • Methods for communicating with students, staff and families.
  • Arrangements for students who need assistance.
  • Attendance checking and accounting for students after evacuation.
  • Periodic training, mock drills and review of identified weaknesses.

For example, during a planned fire-evacuation drill, teachers guide students through the designated safe route to an assembly area and account for them. An exercise may reveal an obstructed exit, unclear instructions or delays in assisting particular students. Those findings should lead to improvements.

Precautions depend on the hazard. During earthquake shaking, the standard public protective action in an appropriate indoor setting is Drop, Cover and Hold On; people should not automatically rush towards exits while the shaking continues. For a fire, the relevant evacuation arrangements are different.

The National Disaster Management Authority issued its National Disaster Management Guidelines on School Safety Policy in February 2016. Gujarat has also implemented school-safety initiatives involving awareness activities, disaster management plans, teacher training and mock drills.

Hospital disaster management plans

Hospitals must protect patients and staff while maintaining essential health services. This makes hospital preparedness different from ordinary building evacuation.

Some patients have limited mobility or depend on continuous medical support. A hospital plan must therefore consider how services can continue when electricity, water, communication, supplies or access routes are disrupted.

Important elements include:

  • Defined responsibilities and internal communication arrangements.
  • Identification of essential services that must continue during disruption.
  • Backup arrangements for critical utilities and supplies.
  • Coordination with health authorities and other hospitals.
  • Safe arrangements for patients, visitors and staff, including those needing additional assistance.
  • Training, exercises and review of service-continuity arrangements.

Hospital evacuation is not automatically the safest response to every emergency. The appropriate action depends on the hazard, the safety of the facility and the needs of patients. Decisions require responsible hospital and emergency authorities.

NDMA issued its National Disaster Management Guidelines: Hospital Safety in February 2016. Hospital preparedness also reflects the wider principle that essential health care should continue as far as safely possible during emergencies.

Industrial disaster management plans

Industrial facilities may face fires, explosions, hazardous chemical releases and disruption of essential services. Preparedness is particularly important where an incident could affect workers and surrounding communities.

The distinction between on-site and off-site emergency planning is central.

PlanMain area of concernMain responsibility
On-site emergency planEmergencies within the industrial establishmentIndustrial occupier or management, within the applicable regulatory framework
Off-site emergency planPossible effects extending beyond the establishmentDistrict Collector or District Emergency Authority designated by the State Government under the 1989 hazardous-chemicals rules, coordinating with the establishment and other agencies

Consider a hypothetical chemical release at an industrial installation near a residential area. The establishment needs arrangements for protecting its workers and reporting the incident. Public authorities need arrangements for warning and protecting any potentially affected population outside the premises.

These responsibilities must be coordinated because a chemical incident may cross the boundary of an establishment. Public instructions, such as whether to remain indoors or move away, depend on the nature of the hazard and directions issued by the competent authorities.

India's regulatory framework includes the Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules, 1989 and the Chemical Accidents (Emergency Planning, Preparedness and Response) Rules, 1996. The latter provide a framework for crisis-management arrangements relating to chemical accidents.

Comparison of the three sectors

InstitutionPrincipal preparedness concernImportant exercise objective
SchoolProtection and accounting of childrenSafe action, communication and student accountability
HospitalSafety and continuity of essential health careCommunication, service continuity and coordination
IndustryWorker safety and control of effects within and beyond the siteTesting on-site arrangements and coordination with off-site authorities

Prelims focus

  • NDMA issued School Safety Policy guidelines in February 2016.
  • NDMA issued Hospital Safety guidelines in February 2016.
  • School safety plans address hazards, responsibilities, evacuation, student accountability and drills.
  • Hospital preparedness emphasises patient safety and continuity of essential services.
  • Industrial emergency planning distinguishes on-site arrangements from off-site arrangements.
  • Trap: An industrial on-site emergency plan does not replace the need for coordinated planning for possible effects outside the premises.

[Sources: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: School Safety Policy, February 2016; NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Hospital Safety, February 2016; World Health Organization, Hospital Emergency Response Checklist, 9 September 2011, overview and continuity of essential services; Ministry of Environment and Forests, Chemical Accidents (Emergency Planning, Preparedness and Response) Rules, 1996; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, notice on chemical accident rules, 8 August 2016; GSDMA, Chapter XVII, Section 17.1, School Safety Programmes; consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: A school drill helps teachers and students practise their assigned safety arrangements.
